case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) permits a damages suit against the United States/USPS for alleged intentional discrimination and property deprivation by postal employees, or whether the claim is barred by the FTCA’s exceptions (as the government argues) such that the plaintiff is left with no tort remedy.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Tort Claims Act, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1346(b), 2671–2680 (including the FTCA exceptions and their interaction with the Westfall Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2679(b)); referenced constitutional backdrop includes accountability for federal officials and the Constitution-savings clause in § 2679(b)(2)(A).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: USPS and the United States argue that the FTCA does not authorize respondent’s suit because the alleged misconduct falls within an FTCA exception (and/or outside the statute’s waiver of sovereign immunity), so sovereign immunity remains intact and the Fifth Circuit erred by allowing the case to proceed. They also press a narrower reading of the FTCA’s waiver and exceptions consistent with limiting federal exposure to tort liability, emphasizing that courts must strictly construe waivers of sovereign immunity and not expand the FTCA beyond its text and this Court’s precedents.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Konan argues that her claim fits within the FTCA’s waiver and is not barred by any applicable exception when the statute is read in context and in light of this Court’s interpretive approach to the FTCA (including attention to purpose and the overall remedial scheme). Respondent (supported by amici) emphasizes that the modern remedial landscape often makes the FTCA the only viable damages remedy for federal wrongdoing (given limits on Bivens and Westfall Act substitution), so adopting the government’s broad view of the exception would improperly convert the FTCA into ‘nothing’ for many real-world harms and undermine federal accountability.
key_precedents: Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006)
Buchanan v. Barr, 71 F.4th 1003 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (Walker, J., concurring)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest textual point: “any claim arising out of” is broad, and “loss” or “miscarriage” can naturally cover mail that never arrives, regardless of motive. But Dolan, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, did more than draw an injury-versus-cause line; it warned against converting § 2680(b)’s specific triad into an all-purpose postal immunity, and the company “loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” reads to me as targeting the routine operational hazards of mail carriage, not a qualitatively different claim of deliberate, allegedly discriminatory deprivation. I agree with the petitioners that we should not create an intent element out of thin air, yet a minimalist holding can respect the breadth of “arising out of” while still concluding that § 2680(b) does not categorically bar this intentional-deprivation theory at the threshold, leaving other defenses (including scope, causation, and merits) to do their work. The remedial-gap concern flagged by Justice Sotomayor cannot expand the waiver, but it reinforces my reluctance—absent clearer text—to adopt an interpretation that effectively immunizes deliberate misconduct whenever it is implemented through nondelivery.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest counter, pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan, is Dolan’s warning against treating § 2680(b) as an all-purpose bar for any harm involving the mails, and their view that the triad targets routine operational mishaps rather than deliberate wrongdoing. But Dolan’s narrowing was about the causal link between the injury and a delivery failure (slip-and-fall versus mail that “fails to arrive” or is misdelivered), and it reaffirmed that nondelivery-based injuries fall within “loss” or “miscarriage”; here the claimed damages still “aris[e] out of” nondelivery/withholding of postal matter. Justice Kagan’s reliance on “negligent transmission” to imply an accident-only limitation for “loss” and “miscarriage” is inconsistent with the text’s structure—Congress inserted “negligent” only for “transmission,” and we may not add a mens rea carveout to preserve remedies where Congress has reserved immunity. Justice Sotomayor’s remedial-gap concerns after Ziglar and Egbert, while understandable, are policy considerations that cannot narrow an express statutory exception to a waiver of sovereign immunity.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Dolan-based warning against an “all-purpose” mail carveout is the strongest point for respondent, but it does not fit this case because Dolan’s narrowing line was about the injury’s independence from a delivery failure, not about the employee’s motive. Here, as Justice Thomas stresses, the damages “arise out of” the nondelivery itself, which falls within the ordinary meaning of “loss” or “miscarriage,” and Congress’s decision to modify only “transmission” with “negligent” cuts against importing an intent limitation into the other nouns. Justice Kagan’s structural argument (pairing with “negligent transmission”) reads more like a policy gloss than a textual constraint, and in the FTCA context we must strictly enforce exceptions preserving sovereign immunity rather than narrow them to avoid remedial gaps. Remedial-gap concerns noted by Justices Sotomayor and Jackson are real, but under Egbert/Ziglar they cannot justify expanding the waiver by allowing artful pleading to recharacterize nondelivery as a separate intentional tort outside § 2680(b).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest textual point—that “any claim arising out of” is broad and that “loss” or “miscarriage” can linguistically encompass intentional withholding—but Dolan’s narrowing principle is not just about injury type; it reads § 2680(b)’s triad as aimed at routine postal delivery failures, reinforced by Congress’s choice to single out “negligent transmission” as part of that operational cluster. As the Chief Justice notes, we can decide narrowly: this suit’s gravamen is an intentional, allegedly discriminatory deprivation of service, and I’m not persuaded we should treat that as categorically barred at the threshold simply because the mechanism is nondelivery. The petitioners’ “no mens rea limitation” point does not answer the structural inference from the statute’s specific phrasing that Congress was carving out the everyday hazards of postal handling, not conferring near-total immunity for deliberate misuse of delivery functions. Remedial-gap concerns post-Egbert/Ziglar cannot expand a waiver, but they underscore why we should not infer such sweeping immunity without clearer text than these delivery-mishap nouns provide.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is textual: “any claim arising out of” is broad, and “loss”/“miscarriage” can describe nondelivery without regard to motive; Justice Thomas is right that we cannot narrow a sovereign-immunity reservation by remedial-gap policy. But Dolan’s structural cue still matters for me as a pragmatic textualist: the triad “loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” reads as a coherent carveout for the ordinary operational hazards of moving mail, not a categorical bar on qualitatively different wrongdoing (intentional deprivation/discrimination) merely because it culminates in nondelivery. I am not importing a mens rea element into “loss/miscarriage”; I’m reading those terms in context with “negligent transmission” to identify the kind of “loss/miscarriage” Congress had in view, consistent with Dolan’s refusal to let § 2680(b) become an all-purpose mail-related immunity. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow holding—that § 2680(b) does not categorically bar this intentional-deprivation theory at the threshold—best preserves statutory coherence while leaving other defenses and merits questions for later.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest point on the other side is Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s reading of Dolan as a warning against an “all-purpose” postal carveout, but Dolan’s narrowing principle turned on the causal source of the injury (independent slip-and-fall versus harms traceable to nondelivery/misdelivery), not on importing an intent-based limitation into “loss” or “miscarriage.” As Justice Thomas stresses, Congress barred “any claim arising out of” a “loss” or “miscarriage” of postal matter—language that naturally captures damages flowing from withheld or misdelivered mail, however the plaintiff labels the theory. Justice Kagan’s reliance on the phrase “negligent transmission” cannot do the work she assigns it, because Congress chose to modify only “transmission,” and under ordinary textual inference we should not add a negligence requirement to the unmodified nouns “loss” and “miscarriage.” Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s remedial-gap concern after Ziglar/Egbert is understandable, but separation-of-powers principles forbid us from narrowing an express sovereign-immunity reservation to improve remedies where Congress used broad causal and categorical terms.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest respondent point, pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan, is Dolan’s warning against reading § 2680(b) as an all-purpose postal immunity and their view that the triad targets routine operational mishaps. But Dolan’s actual dividing line was causal—injuries independent of delivery failure versus injuries traceable to mail that fails to arrive or is misdelivered—and here the alleged harm still “aris[es] out of” the nondelivery/withholding of “postal matter,” which fits the ordinary meaning of “loss” or “miscarriage” as Justice Thomas emphasizes. I do not think we can use Dolan’s anti-sweep rhetoric to insert an intent-based or wrong-kind limitation into “loss” and “miscarriage,” especially when Congress chose to add “negligent” only to “transmission” and used the broad “any claim arising out of” connector. Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s remedial-gap concerns after Abbasi/Egbert are serious as a policy matter, but under strict construction of a waiver “subject to” enumerated exceptions, they cannot justify narrowing an immunity-preserving exception beyond its textual and historically ordinary scope.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest contrary point is Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on Dolan’s admonition against turning § 2680(b) into an all-purpose mail carveout, and their effort to confine the exception to routine operational mishaps. But Dolan’s narrowing principle was about the kind of injury—independent of mail failure versus traceable to nondelivery/misdirection—and Dolan expressly described the exception as covering mail that “fails to arrive at all … or at the wrong address,” which is the causal source alleged here. Justice Kagan’s structural argument from the modifier “negligent” before “transmission” cannot, as a textual matter, supply an implied intent limitation for the unmodified nouns “loss” and “miscarriage,” especially given the sweeping causal language “any claim arising out of.” The remedial-gap concerns emphasized by Justices Sotomayor and Jackson are weighty, but under the FTCA’s waiver “subject to” enumerated exceptions, those policy consequences cannot narrow an immunity-preserving exception beyond its ordinary public meaning or allow artful pleading to evade it, as Justice Thomas notes.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is textual: “any claim arising out of” is broad, and “loss” or “miscarriage” can linguistically cover mail that never arrives, regardless of intent. But Dolan, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, does more than draw a mere injury/causation line; it instructs us to read § 2680(b) as a targeted carveout for the ordinary operational hazards of mail delivery, and the pairing of “loss, miscarriage” with “negligent transmission” reinforces that Congress was not silently immunizing deliberate, allegedly discriminatory interference simply because it is implemented through the mails. Justice Gorsuch’s artful-pleading concern doesn’t overcome that structural reading because the gravamen here is purposeful deprivation (a qualitatively different wrong), not routine nondelivery—so applying § 2680(b) categorically at the threshold would, in practical effect, convert a specific exception into near-blanket postal immunity. I therefore would affirm that § 2680(b) does not foreclose jurisdiction over this intentional-deprivation theory, leaving other defenses and merits issues to subsequent stages.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FTCA’s postal-matter exception preserves immunity only for claims “arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of mail, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(b), and in Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv. we rejected an atextually broad reading that would sweep in all mail-related harms. Reading § 2680(b) in light of its specific terms and its narrower phrasing compared to neighboring § 2680 exceptions supports treating alleged intentional discrimination and purposeful deprivation as outside the exception’s core (loss/miscarriage/negligent transmission). That narrow construction respects precedent and avoids an expansive immunity rule that would effectively eliminate the FTCA remedy for a common category of wrongful conduct—particularly significant given the modern limits on implied constitutional damages remedies (Egbert; Ziglar). On minimal grounds, the Fifth Circuit should be affirmed insofar as it allowed the FTCA claim to proceed past the postal exception, without opining on broader constitutional or Bivens questions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FTCA is a limited waiver of sovereign immunity and must be construed strictly according to its text, and § 2680(b) withdraws that waiver for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.” Read in its ordinary public meaning, a claim predicated on postal employees’ actions that result in mail being withheld, misdelivered, or otherwise not delivered as intended “arises out of” a “loss” or “miscarriage” of postal matter, regardless of whether the employee’s conduct is characterized as intentional discrimination. Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv. confirms the exception covers injuries arising because mail “fails to arrive at all or arrives late, in damaged condition, or at the wrong address,” and respondent’s theory seeks damages for precisely that kind of non-delivery/property deprivation rather than for an independent tort like the slip-and-fall in Dolan. Whatever remedial gap remains is for Congress to address; courts may not expand the FTCA’s waiver beyond § 2680(b)’s textual limits, and the narrowing of implied constitutional remedies in Egbert and Ziglar reinforces that the judiciary should not create substitute damages regimes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver is limited by its enumerated exceptions, and § 2680(b) bars “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.” Under Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006), those terms are best read to cover core delivery failures—mail that fails to arrive, is misdelivered, or is otherwise lost in the course of postal operations—and respondent’s alleged property deprivation fits comfortably within that category. Allowing plaintiffs to recharacterize nondelivery or loss of mail as intentional discrimination would circumvent Congress’s chosen immunity boundary and expose USPS to expansive tort liability inconsistent with the FTCA’s structure and practical consequences for nationwide mail operations. Given the Court’s reluctance to create alternative damages remedies against federal officers (Egbert v. Boule; Ziglar v. Abbasi), the absence of a remedy here is a policy matter for Congress, not a basis to narrow § 2680(b) beyond its text.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2680(b)’s postal-matter exception preserves immunity only for claims “arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of mail, and Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006), instructs that FTCA exceptions should not be read so broadly that they swallow the waiver—especially where Congress used comparatively narrow, specific language. On these allegations (intentional discrimination and deliberate deprivation rather than inadvertent misdelivery or negligent handling), the claim is plausibly outside § 2680(b)’s limited scope and thus within the FTCA’s general waiver in § 1346(b), leaving the United States answerable for wrongful acts “under circumstances where” a private person would be liable. Given the modern remedial landscape after Abbasi and Egbert sharply restricting Bivens and the Westfall Act’s substitution regime in § 2679(b), adopting the government’s expansive exception would too often leave victims—particularly vulnerable individuals—without any damages remedy for concrete harms. The better reading, consistent with Dolan and the FTCA’s remedial purpose, is that sovereign immunity does not bar this suit at the threshold on the government’s theory of the exception.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2680(b) preserves immunity only for claims “arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of mail, and Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv. read that language narrowly, emphasizing Congress’s choice of specific terms rather than a sweeping carveout for all USPS mail-handling torts. On the allegations here—intentional discrimination and deliberate property deprivation by postal employees—the better textual fit is that the claim does not arise from “negligent transmission” and is not the kind of accidental “loss” or “miscarriage” Congress targeted, so it remains within the FTCA’s waiver in § 1346(b). That reading also coheres with the FTCA/Westfall Act remedial structure in § 2679(b): broadening § 2680(b) to cover intentional wrongdoing would often leave plaintiffs with no damages remedy given the Court’s limits on implied constitutional actions in Ziglar v. Abbasi and Egbert v. Boule. The statute’s text and workability thus favor allowing the FTCA claim to proceed absent a clearer exception.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver is limited, and § 2680(b) preserves sovereign immunity for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter,” which—read by its ordinary meaning and as construed in Dolan—covers harms traceable to nondelivery, misdelivery, or other failures in the postal obligation to deliver to the right address. Even if the complaint is styled as intentional discrimination or property deprivation, if the injury “arises out of” the loss or miscarriage of mail, the postal exception applies and courts may not expand the waiver beyond Congress’s text. Nor may we manufacture a tort remedy because other avenues (including Bivens after Ziglar and Egbert) are constrained; separation of powers requires leaving any remedial gap to Congress. Given the FTCA’s strict conditions on suit against the sovereign and the specific postal exception’s scope as recognized in Dolan, the Fifth Circuit’s allowance of the claim cannot stand.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver of sovereign immunity must be strictly construed, and § 2680(b) preserves immunity for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of mail. Under Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., that exception covers injuries arising “directly or consequentially” because mail “fails to arrive at all,” and the alleged intentional refusal to deliver is still a claim “arising out of” nondelivery within the ordinary meaning of “loss” or “miscarriage.” Whatever the policy concern about remedial gaps in light of limits on Bivens (Egbert; Ziglar), it is for Congress—not the Court—to expand the FTCA beyond the text of its exceptions. Accordingly, sovereign immunity remains intact and the Fifth Circuit erred in allowing the FTCA suit to proceed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver in 28 U.S.C. § 1346(b)(1) is expressly “[s]ubject to” the exceptions in § 2680, and § 2680(b) withdraws jurisdiction for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.” Under Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., that exception is read to cover injuries arising because mail fails to arrive, arrives late, damaged, or misdelivered, and respondent’s alleged harms stem from nondelivery/misdirection of mail—i.e., a “miscarriage” of postal matter within the ordinary meaning of the text. Because waivers of sovereign immunity must be strictly construed and courts may not expand the FTCA beyond its terms, the statutory exception controls even if it leaves respondent without an FTCA tort remedy; the Westfall Act’s preservation of certain constitutional claims in § 2679(b)(2)(A) does not enlarge the FTCA’s waiver where § 2680(b) applies. Accordingly, sovereign immunity remains intact as to this suit, and the Fifth Circuit erred in allowing it to proceed.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FTCA is a remedial waiver of sovereign immunity, and its exceptions must be read in context and not “stretched to the outer limits of [their] definitional possibilities,” particularly where doing so would convert the waiver into a near-nullity for commonplace, real-world harms. Dolan v. USPS construed the postal exception in 28 U.S.C. § 2680(b) narrowly, emphasizing Congress’s choice of more specific language than neighboring “any claim arising out of” exceptions, which counsels against the government’s broad immunity theory here. Given the Westfall Act’s substitution rule, 28 U.S.C. § 2679(b), and the sharp limitations on Bivens remedies after Ziglar v. Abbasi and Egbert v. Boule, adopting the government’s expansive reading would leave the plaintiff with no damages remedy at all—an outcome in tension with the FTCA’s structure and Congress’s evident accountability aims. On this record and statutory backdrop, I would allow the suit to proceed absent a clear, textually compelled exception that squarely covers intentional discrimination and property deprivation as alleged.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) bars respondent’s tort suit against the United States Postal Service because the alleged misconduct falls within an FTCA exception that preserves federal sovereign immunity.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Tort Claims Act (28 U.S.C. §§ 1346(b), 2671–2680), particularly the scope of FTCA waiver and its statutory exceptions (28 U.S.C. § 2680), as applied to claims arising from alleged intentional discrimination and property deprivation by federal employees; related background includes the Westfall Act (28 U.S.C. § 2679).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The government (USPS and related petitioners) argues that even if the complaint alleges wrongful conduct by postal employees, the FTCA’s waiver does not reach these claims because one or more FTCA exceptions in § 2680 apply. Under the government’s reading, when an exception applies, sovereign immunity remains intact and the federal courts lack subject-matter jurisdiction, requiring dismissal. Petitioners also frame respondent and amici as seeking an accountability-expanding construction of the FTCA that conflicts with the statute’s text and this Court’s FTCA exception jurisprudence, and they emphasize that the FTCA is a limited waiver that must be applied as written rather than broadened to fill perceived remedial gaps created by limits on Bivens and other doctrines.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues the Fifth Circuit correctly rejected the government’s attempt to recharacterize the alleged wrong as falling within an FTCA exception, and that the claim fits within the FTCA’s general waiver because it alleges the kind of state-law tort liability that would attach to a private person in analogous circumstances. Respondent and supporting amici (e.g., Institute for Justice, APA Watch, Taxpayers Protection Alliance) emphasize that the government’s position would further hollow out the FTCA—often the only realistic remedy for federal wrongdoing after the contraction of Bivens and the channeling effects of the Westfall Act—creating an accountability deficit inconsistent with the FTCA’s purpose and with interpretive principles that construe FTCA exceptions in a contextual and appropriately limited way.
key_precedents: Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006)
Buchanan v. Barr, 71 F.4th 1003 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (Walker, J., concurring)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor rightly press Dolan’s caution against driving § 2680(b) to its “outer limits,” especially given the remedial gaps after Egbert and the Westfall Act, but Dolan’s narrowing principle was aimed at collateral, non-mail injuries—not at carving out intentional diversion claims whose gravamen is still nonreceipt of mail. Justice Kavanaugh’s grammatical point remains the most persuasive textual constraint: Congress limited only “transmission” with “negligent,” and it is not our role to add an intent limitation to “loss” or “miscarriage” to avoid hard remedial outcomes. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Brownback reinforces the institutional point that once an enumerated § 2680 exception fits, the FTCA waiver does not and we lack authority to proceed, so policy concerns cannot drive a narrowing construction beyond ordinary meaning. Under a minimalist approach, I would hold only that claims predicated on deprivation/nonreceipt of mail—even if pleaded as intentional diversion—“aris[e] out of” a “loss” or “miscarriage” within § 2680(b), while reserving questions about distinct collateral torts or other statutory avenues.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is Dolan’s caution against pressing § 2680(b) to its “outer limits” and their view that Congress was focused on routine delivery mishaps, not intentional discriminatory diversion. But under the ordinary meaning of the text, a claim “arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage” of mail encompasses the deprivation caused by nondelivery or misdelivery regardless of the employee’s intent, and—as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes—the statute’s grammar places “negligent” only before “transmission,” foreclosing an atextual intent limitation for “loss” or “miscarriage.” Dolan’s contextual narrowing, as the Chief Justice explains, separates collateral injuries from claims whose gravamen is nonreceipt; here the asserted harm is still the failure of the postal matter to arrive, so the exception applies. Justice Jackson’s remedial-gap concern after Egbert is not trivial, but as Brownback confirms the consequence is jurisdictional once an enumerated § 2680 exception fits, and we cannot expand a limited waiver of sovereign immunity by narrowing an exception beyond its original public meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is Dolan’s caution against pushing § 2680(b) to its “outer limits,” especially given the remedial gaps after Egbert and the Westfall Act, but Dolan’s narrowing principle addressed collateral, non-mail harms—not claims whose injury is the very nondelivery/misdelivery of postal matter. As Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, Congress placed “negligent” only before “transmission,” and it is not our role to add an intent limitation to “loss” or “miscarriage” to preserve remedies Congress did not supply. Justice Jackson’s gravamen approach is too malleable in a sovereign-immunity exception and invites artful pleading: the claim still “aris[es] out of” the deprivation of mail, which is precisely what the text covers. Brownback, as Justice Thomas notes, reinforces the institutional point that once § 2680(b) applies the FTCA waiver is unavailable, and remedial-gap concerns cannot justify narrowing an exception beyond its ordinary meaning.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh have the strongest textual point: “negligent” is placed only before “transmission,” so an intent-based carveout is not on the face of the grammar, and their artful-pleading concern is real. But Dolan’s contextual approach still requires us to read “loss” and “miscarriage” in their delivery-mishap setting and to apply “arising out of” to the claim’s gravamen; where the allegation is targeted, independently wrongful deprivation (not a failure in carriage), treating that as categorically a “loss” pushes § 2680(b) to the outer limits Dolan cautioned against and creates a serious accountability gap post-Egbert. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on Brownback does not undercut that threshold characterization question—it speaks to what follows once an exception applies, not whether Congress clearly put this kind of abusive conduct within the postal exception in the first place. Under my pragmatic methodology, absent clearer textual compulsion, I would not extend § 2680(b) to immunize intentional misconduct that uses nondelivery as a tool rather than presenting as a routine postal “loss.”

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s grammatical point—that “negligent” most naturally modifies only “transmission,” leaving “loss” and “miscarriage” not expressly negligence-limited—is strong, and I do not rely on atextually inserting an “intent” carveout. But Dolan’s contextual approach still matters: even if “loss” can be intentional in some abstract sense, in § 2680(b)’s postal-delivery setting (and given Dolan’s warning about “outer limits”), the better reading is that “arising out of” should track the claim’s gravamen and exclude independently wrongful, targeted deprivation where nondelivery is the means, not the mischief Congress meant to immunize. Justice Thomas’s Brownback point clarifies the consequence once § 2680(b) applies, but it does not answer the threshold interpretive question whether Congress used “loss” and “miscarriage” to reach this atypical, discriminatory misuse of the mail system rather than routine failures in carriage. I’m not persuaded that a gravamen-focused “arising out of” inquiry is unadministrable; it is more coherent (and less immunity-expansive) than a rule that effectively makes § 2680(b) a near-categorical bar whenever a postal employee can effectuate wrongdoing through nondelivery.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is Dolan’s caution against reading § 2680(b) to its “outer limits,” especially where the alleged misconduct is intentional and abusive, but Dolan’s contextual narrowing separated collateral torts from claims whose gravamen is nondelivery or misdelivery—not by importing an intent element into “loss” or “miscarriage.” As Justice Kavanaugh stresses, Congress expressly limited only “transmission” with “negligent,” and under ordinary grammar we lack warrant to rewrite the other nouns to mean “negligent loss” or “negligent miscarriage” just to preserve a remedy. Justice Jackson’s accountability-gap concern after Egbert and the Westfall Act is a serious policy problem, yet separation-of-powers principles foreclose narrowing a sovereign-immunity exception beyond its text to fix remedial consequences Congress has chosen. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Brownback does not answer the threshold characterization question, but it reinforces the institutional need for a clear, text-based jurisdictional boundary once an enumerated § 2680 exception applies.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: Dolan’s warning against stretching § 2680(b) to its “outer limits” and the concern that an expansive reading creates an accountability gap for intentional, abusive diversion. But Dolan’s limiting move, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, was to exclude collateral, non-mail injuries—not to rewrite “loss” and “miscarriage” to mean only routine negligence—especially when Congress placed “negligent” only before “transmission,” a structural choice that strongly counsels against importing an intent-based carveout. Justice Sotomayor’s proposed gravamen/intent line is also not administrable in a sovereign-immunity exception: it invites artful pleading and turns a categorical jurisdictional boundary into an intent inquiry we are poorly situated to police. Brownback (as Justice Thomas notes) does not answer the antecedent fit question, but it reinforces the institutional point that once § 2680(b) covers the claim’s core injury—nonreceipt/misdelivery of mail—dismissal must follow and any remedial gap is for Congress, not this Court, to close.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is Dolan’s admonition not to extend § 2680(b) to its “outer limits,” especially given the remedial gaps after Egbert and the Westfall Act; but Dolan’s limiting move was to exclude collateral, non-mail harms from the postal exception, not to create an intent-based carveout where the injury remains the deprivation/nonreceipt of mail. As Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, the statute’s grammar is telling: Congress placed “negligent” only before “transmission,” and it is difficult under ordinary meaning to read “loss” and “miscarriage” as silently confined to negligent mishaps without adding words. The respondents’ proposed “gravamen” approach risks becoming atextual and administratively unstable in a sovereign-immunity waiver, inviting artful pleading whenever intentional misconduct is alleged alongside nondelivery. Brownback, as Justice Thomas notes, does not answer the threshold interpretive question, but it reinforces that once § 2680(b) applies, we must dismiss regardless of remedial desirability, which is a matter for Congress.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and the Chief Justice’s grammatical point—that “negligent” modifies only “transmission,” not “loss” or “miscarriage”—is the strongest case for Petitioner, and I agree we should not invent an atextual intent carveout. But that point does not resolve the antecedent question Dolan foregrounds: what Congress meant by “loss” in a delivery-focused exception, and whether a targeted, independently wrongful deprivation is properly characterized as a postal “loss” rather than misconduct merely using the mail as an instrumentality. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Brownback underscores the consequence once § 2680(b) clearly applies, yet it does not answer the gravamen/“arising out of” characterization issue at the threshold, where the government bears the burden to show this atypical claim fits squarely within the exception. Given Dolan’s warning against pushing § 2680(b) to its outer limits, I do not think text-plus-context compels extending “loss” to cover deliberate, abusive diversion in a way that risks broad immunity beyond routine nondelivery/misdelivery mishaps.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FTCA is a limited waiver of sovereign immunity, and when an exception in 28 U.S.C. § 2680 applies, the waiver does not extend to the claim and the suit must be dismissed. Here, respondent’s theory—an intentional deprivation or diversion of mail by postal employees—still “aris[es] out of the loss [or] miscarriage … of letters or postal matter” within § 2680(b), and Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv. instructs that the postal-matter exception covers injuries tied to mail delivery failures rather than collateral negligence like a slip-and-fall. Reading “loss” and “miscarriage” to exclude intentional deprivations would invite claim-recharacterization and undermine administrable, narrow jurisdictional lines in a statute that must be applied as written. While the contraction of Bivens remedies (Egbert; Ziglar) may leave gaps, that policy concern cannot justify expanding the FTCA beyond its text or exceptions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FTCA is a limited waiver of sovereign immunity and must be applied according to its text; if a claim falls within an exception in 28 U.S.C. § 2680, “the bar of sovereign immunity remains.” Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481, 485 (2006). Section 2680(b) preserves immunity for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of mail, and Dolan explained that this exception generally covers injuries arising directly or consequentially because mail fails to arrive, arrives late, damaged, or at the wrong address. Where the pleaded harm is fundamentally tied to nondelivery or misdelivery (i.e., “loss” or “miscarriage”), the exception applies and federal courts lack jurisdiction notwithstanding policy arguments about remedial gaps. Consistent with Brownback v. King, 592 U.S. 209 (2021), the court must dismiss when the statutory conditions for the waiver are not met because an exception restores immunity.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver in § 1346(b)(1) is expressly “[s]ubject to” the exceptions in § 2680, and § 2680(b) provides that § 1346(b) “shall not apply to” claims arising out of the “loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of postal matter—thus preserving sovereign immunity when the exception fits. Consistent with Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., the postal exception must be applied according to its text and structure, and it would be anomalous to read “loss” narrowly in § 2680(b) when the same term in the FTCA framework refers broadly to deprivations, including those caused by intentional misconduct. Given that this is a limited waiver and exceptions define the retained immunity, the practical consequence of respondent’s reading would be an unwarranted expansion of liability beyond what Congress authorized, especially where alternative remedies are for Congress to supply. Under Brownback v. King, when an FTCA exception applies, the court lacks authority to proceed and dismissal is required.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver applies where a private person would face analogous state-law tort liability, and § 2680 exceptions should not be expanded by relabeling the gravamen of the claim to fit an immunity-preserving category. Under Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006), § 2680(b) is construed with attention to Congress’s comparatively narrow phrasing—targeting losses and negligent transmission incidents tied to ordinary mail-handling mishaps—rather than sweeping in all USPS misconduct that happens to affect delivery. Where the alleged wrongdoing is intentional discrimination or targeted deprivation by employees, treating it as merely “loss” or “miscarriage” risks creating an accountability gap, especially after the contraction of Bivens remedies (Ziglar v. Abbasi; Egbert v. Boule) and the channeling effects of the Westfall Act, and that is not compelled by the text of § 2680(b). Accordingly, I would affirm jurisdiction and allow the suit to proceed under the FTCA’s general waiver rather than broaden the exception beyond Dolan’s limiting principles.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FTCA waives immunity for state-law tort claims against the United States, 28 U.S.C. § 1346(b), and its exceptions in § 2680 must be read in light of the whole statutory text and context rather than stretched to their “outer limits.” Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006), rejected an expansive construction of the postal exception and emphasized Congress’s comparatively narrow wording in § 2680(b) versus neighboring, broader exceptions, supporting a limited reading that targets routine mail-delivery mishaps. On this record (alleged intentional discrimination and property deprivation via misuse of postal processes), the government’s recharacterization would convert a targeted exception into a near-categorical bar for USPS misconduct, undermining statutory coherence and workability where FTCA remedies often substitute for foreclosed individual-capacity suits after the Westfall Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2679. Consistent with Dolan and the structure of § 2680, I would hold the exception does not clearly cover this atypical, intentional abuse and the suit is not barred on that ground.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FTCA is a limited waiver of sovereign immunity, and courts must respect the limits Congress wrote, including the categorical exceptions in 28 U.S.C. § 2680; when an exception applies, “section 1346(b) shall not apply,” and the suit cannot proceed. Whatever the policy concerns about remedial gaps after Bivens, that is not a license to narrow statutory exceptions beyond their text or to expand the waiver by judicial gloss—separation-of-powers principles require that any further remedy come from Congress. Dolan confirms that § 2680(b) is not boundless, but it also teaches we must follow the statute’s specific language and structure as a coherent whole; if the alleged injury arises from the kind of mail-handling/property-loss conduct Congress excepted, sovereign immunity remains. Consistent with Brownback v. King, the FTCA’s jurisdictional grant and its exceptions define the court’s authority, so an applicable § 2680 exception requires dismissal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FTCA is a limited waiver of sovereign immunity, and when an enumerated exception in 28 U.S.C. § 2680 applies, the waiver does not extend to the claim and the suit must be dismissed. Here, the alleged misconduct centers on deprivation of postal matter and therefore “aris[es] out of the loss … of letters or postal matter” within § 2680(b), which by its text is not confined to negligent deprivations (Congress used “negligent” only to modify “transmission,” not “loss”). Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006), instructs that § 2680 exceptions should be read in a text- and context-grounded way—cabined from overexpansion, but still applied as written—and that approach supports treating this as a paradigmatic “loss of mail” claim. Practical workability also favors a clear rule that channels mail-loss disputes away from FTCA litigation, rather than turning such cases into intent-based line-drawing that Congress did not codify in § 2680(b).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FTCA is a limited waiver of sovereign immunity, and when an exception in 28 U.S.C. § 2680 applies, immunity is retained and the suit must be dismissed. Section 2680(b) preserves immunity for claims arising out of the “loss,” “miscarriage,” or “negligent transmission” of postal matter, and under Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006), that exception covers harms stemming from nondelivery or misdelivery—paradigmatically including consequential harms from failure of mail to arrive. To the extent respondent’s theory depends on postal employees’ handling (or non-handling) of mail resulting in loss or nondelivery, the claim falls within § 2680(b) regardless of how it is pleaded, and Brownback v. King, 592 U.S. 209 (2021), underscores that the FTCA’s jurisdictional grant does not extend to claims excluded by § 2680. Whatever remedial gap exists after the contraction of Bivens (Egbert v. Boule, 596 U.S. 482 (2022)), it cannot justify expanding the FTCA beyond the statute’s text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FTCA waives sovereign immunity for state-law torts, and its exceptions in 28 U.S.C. § 2680 must be read in context and not stretched “to the outer limits of [their] definitional possibilities,” particularly where doing so would nullify the statute’s remedial design. Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006), counsels that the postal-related exception (§ 2680(b)) is comparatively specific and should be cabined to routine mishandling or transmission problems, not leveraged to recharacterize atypical, intentional misconduct (such as discriminatory or abusive property deprivation) into immunity-preserving “mail” claims. Given the narrowing of Bivens remedies (Egbert v. Boule, 596 U.S. 482 (2022)), an overbroad reading of § 2680 would create a substantial accountability gap inconsistent with Congress’s chosen FTCA framework and basic procedural fairness. On this record, the government has not shown that the alleged wrong squarely falls within an applicable § 2680 exception, so the suit should not be barred at the threshold.
